metadata.narrative: We're a 12-person SaaS team trying to add an internal AI assistant over product docs, tickets, and a few admin APIs. The prototype works with raw OpenAI calls, but now everyone is arguing about whether we should standardize on LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, Semantic Kernel, DSPy, or just keep things custom. We mostly use Python and TypeScript, but our billing/admin systems are .NET. What should we choose for a first production version, and what tradeoffs should we care about for RAG quality, agents/API actions, debugging, evaluation, deployment, and avoiding a framework mess later?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: For a twelve-person team shipping a first production assistant over docs, tickets, and admin APIs, the strongest path is to pick one thin orchestration layer for the Python/TypeScript side rather than trying to standardize every language on one framework, because the frameworks under discussion solve different problems and none cleanly spans Python, TypeScript, and.NET at once.

LlamaIndex is the strongest fit specifically for RAG quality because it is built around data connectors, multiple index types, a LlamaParse pipeline for complex PDFs with tables, and its own evaluation and instrumentation modules covering correctness, faithfulness, and retrieval metrics like MRR and hit rate.

A direct comparison frames the core tradeoff: LlamaIndex specializes in ingesting, structuring, and rapidly retrieving domain-specific data, while LangChain focuses on chaining and orchestrating multi-step pipelines, so the choice hinges on whether retrieval quality or workflow orchestration matters more first.

For agent behavior and admin API actions, LangChain's ecosystem is the most capable option because LangGraph adds graph-based multi-agent workflows with cycles, state, and custom tool integration, fully integrated with LangSmith observability.

LangGraph's comparison against Autogen and CrewAI shows the tradeoff: graph-based control gives more precise transition control for complex, tool-heavy workflows, while conversation-style frameworks are simpler for looser collaboration.

Haystack 2.0, by contrast, explicitly lacks an Agent abstraction, only approximating agentic behavior via pipeline loops, so it is weaker where tool-calling over admin APIs is a first-class requirement.

Semantic Kernel fits your polyglot reality best, since it natively orchestrates existing C#, Python, and Java code as callable "plugins," making it the natural choice if.NET billing/admin systems need in-process AI orchestration rather than calling out to a separate service.

Semantic Kernel's planners sequence plugin calls into a plan, and its own FAQ distinguishes it from LangChain and LlamaIndex as an orchestration SDK built around plugins and planners rather than a data-retrieval or multi-agent-collaboration framework.

On debugging, LangChain's documentation frames the split cleanly: LangChain is for prototyping, and LangSmith is the production platform for stepping through chains, testing, evaluating, and monitoring, complementing the simpler stepwise debug mode used early on.

Haystack 2.0 was rebuilt with production debugging in mind, adding structured logging with built-in tracing correlation plus a Hayhooks deployment layer that auto-generates REST schemas from pipeline introspection.
LlamaIndex's instrumentation module tracks spans and events through a dispatcher/handler system, giving visibility into retrieval and generation steps.

Framework-agnostic tools like OpenLLMetry and Traceloop can observe vector-database and LLM calls regardless of orchestration layer, which matters if debugging tooling needs to survive a later framework swap.

For evaluation, RAGAS (faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision/recall) and TruLens's RAG Triad (context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance) are the two most established metric sets, and both work largely without hand-labeled ground truth.
The broader tooling landscape also includes Phoenix, DeepEval, LangSmith, and OpenAI Evals, implementing similar metrics with different integration depth into specific frameworks.
LlamaIndex bakes several of these same categories directly into its own evaluation modules, so adopting it for retrieval yields evaluation largely for free.

DSPy is a fundamentally different tool and should be treated as an optimization layer rather than an orchestration replacement: it separates program flow from prompt/weight parameters and uses optimizers plus Assertions to tune prompts against a metric you define.

This is documented to work best in English and to struggle with very complex, highly detailed task instructions, making DSPy a reasonable second-stage investment once evaluation data exists rather than a first production framework.

On avoiding a framework mess later, a practical account of running Haystack, LangChain, and LlamaIndex in production concluded that a custom, dependency-light integration is often the better call, ranking Haystack as the most stable off-the-shelf option and LangChain as flexible but prone to breaking changes across updates.

A more architectural warning is that the biggest lock-in risk is not the vendor chosen but building a universal LLM abstraction at the model-API layer, which forces a lowest-common-denominator interface and blocks fast adoption of new provider features; the fix is keeping any abstraction aligned to specific product user stories instead of to models.

This argues for using LangChain's components selectively, since its own strength is that pieces can be used independently of the full framework, while keeping the assistant's core logic in your own code so a future migration touches call sites rather than the whole application.

Even LangGraph's own comparison discussion acknowledges the broader criticism that LLM frameworks tend to "over-complicate things," reinforcing that added abstraction should be adopted deliberately per capability, not wholesale.

Putting this together for a first production version: build the RAG and agent core in Python using LangChain plus LangGraph for tool-calling over ticket/doc data and admin APIs, instrumented with LangSmith for tracing and RAGAS/TruLens for evaluation.
If retrieval quality over product docs is the primary bottleneck, swap in LlamaIndex's indexing/retrieval layer under that same orchestration rather than replacing the whole stack.

Expose the.NET billing/admin systems as narrow REST endpoints that the Python agent calls as tools, and only reach for Semantic Kernel on the.NET side later if native in-process C# AI orchestration is needed.

Hold off on DSPy and on a dependency-free rebuild until real evaluation data exists and a concrete pain point remains, then let those metrics decide between DSPy-style optimization or a leaner custom layer.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

tools.name: search
tools.description: Search the available evidence corpus. Results contain ranked document IDs and document text; inspect that text directly and cite by docid. Each result is bounded independently before it is staged.

query.description: A natural-language query for evidence relevant to the research request.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

budget_tokens_per_result.description: Maximum approximate tokens staged per result. Text is bounded at tokens × 5 characters and cut at the final line break before that boundary. Default 4096.

tools.name: commit_context
tools.description: Select the small subset of documents from the MOST RECENT staged search batch whose full text should persist. This MUST be the first control action on the immediately following model turn. Every staged occurrence not listed is compacted before the next turn. Do not select a docid that is already committed, or a semantically redundant document supporting the same claim, unless it adds materially different evidence.

documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

reason.description: The distinct evidence, claim, perspective, date, name, counter-evidence, or coverage area this document uniquely contributes.

output.text:
For a twelve-person team shipping a first production assistant over docs, tickets, and admin APIs, the strongest path is to pick one thin orchestration layer for the Python/TypeScript side rather than trying to standardize every language on one framework, because the frameworks under discussion solve different problems and none of them cleanly spans Python, TypeScript, and .NET at once.

LlamaIndex is the strongest fit specifically for RAG quality because it is purpose-built around data connectors, multiple index types, and a LlamaParse pipeline for complex PDFs with tables, plus its own evaluation and instrumentation modules for correctness, faithfulness, and retrieval metrics like MRR and hit rate.
[06182_32791]
One direct comparison frames this precisely: LlamaIndex specializes in ingesting, structuring, and rapidly retrieving domain-specific data, while LangChain focuses on chaining and orchestrating multi-step LLM-driven pipelines, so the choice is really about which 80% of your architecture (retrieval quality versus workflow orchestration) matters most first.
[01599_30573]

For agent behavior and admin API actions, LangChain's ecosystem is the most capable single option because LangGraph adds explicit graph-based multi-agent workflows with cycles, state, and custom tool integration, and it is fully integrated with LangChain's tooling and LangSmith observability.
[05383_29823]
LangGraph's own comparison against Autogen and CrewAI shows the mental-model tradeoff: graph-based control gives more precise control over transition probabilities for complex, tool-heavy workflows, while conversation-style frameworks are simpler to reason about for looser collaboration.
[05383_29823]
By contrast, Haystack 2.0 explicitly does not offer an Agent abstraction, only loop-based approximations inside pipelines, so if agentic tool-calling over your admin APIs is a first-class requirement, Haystack alone is a weaker choice today.
[04375_16829]
Semantic Kernel is the one framework built for your actual polyglot reality, since it natively supports orchestrating existing C#, Python, and Java code as callable "plugins" that an LLM can invoke, making it the natural fit if your .NET billing/admin systems need direct in-process AI orchestration rather than calling out to a Python service.
[06380_51127]
Semantic Kernel's planners generate step-by-step plans that select and sequence plugins, and its own FAQ distinguishes it from LangChain and LlamaIndex by noting it is an orchestration SDK built around plugins and planners rather than a data-retrieval framework or a multi-agent collaboration framework like AutoGen.
[01097_53780]

On debugging, LangChain's own documentation frames the split cleanly: LangChain is for prototyping, and LangSmith is the production-grade platform for stepping through chains, testing, evaluating, and monitoring, complementing the simpler `langchain.debug=True` stepwise inspection used early on.
[04983_23951]
Haystack 2.0 was rebuilt with production debugging in mind, adding customizable structured logging with built-in tracing correlation, plus a lightweight Hayhooks deployment layer that auto-generates REST schemas from pipeline introspection.
[04778_23225]
LlamaIndex's instrumentation module similarly tracks spans and events through a dispatcher/handler system, giving visibility into retrieval and generation steps for debugging and performance tuning.
[06182_32791]
For framework-agnostic tracing, tools like OpenLLMetry and Traceloop can observe calls to vector databases and LLMs regardless of which orchestration layer you pick, which matters if you want debugging tooling that survives a future framework swap.
[01120_44772]

For evaluation, the RAGAS score (faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision/recall) and TruLens's RAG Triad (context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance) are the two most established metric sets and both work largely without hand-labeled ground truth.
[01120_44772]
Beyond these two, the broader tooling landscape includes Phoenix, DeepEval, LangSmith, and OpenAI Evals, each implementing similar ground-truth and no-ground-truth metrics with different integration depth into specific frameworks.
[03736_71037]
LlamaIndex bakes several of these same evaluation categories (correctness, semantic similarity, faithfulness, guideline adherence) directly into its own evaluation modules, so if you adopt LlamaIndex for retrieval you get evaluation largely for free rather than bolting on a separate tool.
[06182_32791]

DSPy is a fundamentally different tool and should be treated as an optimization layer rather than an orchestration replacement: it separates program flow from prompt/weight parameters and uses optimizers ("teleprompters") plus Assertions to automatically tune prompts against a metric you define, which is powerful once you have evaluation data but is documented to work best in English and to struggle with very complex, highly detailed task instructions.
[04975_55112] [05633_69568]
That makes DSPy a reasonable second-stage investment for optimizing your retrieval/generation prompts once RAGAS- or TruLens-style metrics exist, not a first production framework.
[05633_69568]

On avoiding a framework mess later, one practical account from actually running Haystack, LangChain, and LlamaIndex in production concluded that a custom, dependency-light integration is often the better call, ranking Haystack as the most stable of the three off-the-shelf options and LangChain as flexible but prone to breaking changes across updates.
[02086_49022]
A separate, more architectural warning is that the biggest lock-in risk is not choosing the "wrong" vendor but building a universal LLM abstraction at the model-API layer itself, which forces a lowest-common-denominator interface and blocks fast adoption of new provider features; the recommended fix is to keep any abstraction aligned to specific product user stories instead of to models.
[00552_21069]
Practically, this argues for using LangChain's modular components selectively (its own strength is that pieces can be used independently of the full framework) while keeping the assistant's core logic in your own code, so a future migration touches call sites rather than your entire application.
[05567_17824]
Consistent with that, even LangGraph's own comparison discussion acknowledges the broader criticism that LLM frameworks tend to "over-complicate things," reinforcing that added abstraction should be adopted deliberately per capability, not wholesale.
[04066_44043]

Putting this together for a first production version: build the RAG and agent core in Python using LangChain plus LangGraph for tool-calling over your ticket/doc data and admin APIs, instrumented with LangSmith for tracing and RAGAS/TruLens for evaluation, since this combination covers agents, debugging, and evaluation with mature tooling.
[05383_29823] [04983_23951] [01120_44772]
If retrieval quality over the product docs is the primary bottleneck, swap in LlamaIndex's indexing/retrieval layer under that same LangChain/LangGraph orchestration rather than replacing the whole stack.
[06182_32791]
Expose the .NET billing/admin systems as narrow, well-documented REST endpoints that the Python agent calls as tools, and only reach for Semantic Kernel on the .NET side later if you need native in-process AI orchestration inside C#, since Semantic Kernel's plugin model already fits that specific gap.
[06380_51127]
Hold off on DSPy and on any custom, dependency-free rebuild until you have real evaluation data and a concrete pain point that the LangChain/LangGraph/LlamaIndex combination cannot solve, at which point the same evaluation metrics can guide whether DSPy-style prompt optimization or a leaner custom layer is worth the migration cost.
[05633_69568] [02086_49022]

answer.text: For a twelve-person team shipping a first production assistant over docs, tickets, and admin APIs, the strongest path is to pick one thin orchestration layer for the Python/TypeScript side rather than trying to standardize every language on one framework, because the frameworks under discussion solve different problems and none cleanly spans Python, TypeScript, and.NET at once.

LlamaIndex is the strongest fit specifically for RAG quality because it is built around data connectors, multiple index types, a LlamaParse pipeline for complex PDFs with tables, and its own evaluation and instrumentation modules covering correctness, faithfulness, and retrieval metrics like MRR and hit rate.

A direct comparison frames the core tradeoff: LlamaIndex specializes in ingesting, structuring, and rapidly retrieving domain-specific data, while LangChain focuses on chaining and orchestrating multi-step pipelines, so the choice hinges on whether retrieval quality or workflow orchestration matters more first.

For agent behavior and admin API actions, LangChain's ecosystem is the most capable option because LangGraph adds graph-based multi-agent workflows with cycles, state, and custom tool integration, fully integrated with LangSmith observability.

LangGraph's comparison against Autogen and CrewAI shows the tradeoff: graph-based control gives more precise transition control for complex, tool-heavy workflows, while conversation-style frameworks are simpler for looser collaboration.

Haystack 2.0, by contrast, explicitly lacks an Agent abstraction, only approximating agentic behavior via pipeline loops, so it is weaker where tool-calling over admin APIs is a first-class requirement.

Semantic Kernel fits your polyglot reality best, since it natively orchestrates existing C#, Python, and Java code as callable "plugins," making it the natural choice if.NET billing/admin systems need in-process AI orchestration rather than calling out to a separate service.

Semantic Kernel's planners sequence plugin calls into a plan, and its own FAQ distinguishes it from LangChain and LlamaIndex as an orchestration SDK built around plugins and planners rather than a data-retrieval or multi-agent-collaboration framework.

On debugging, LangChain's documentation frames the split cleanly: LangChain is for prototyping, and LangSmith is the production platform for stepping through chains, testing, evaluating, and monitoring, complementing the simpler stepwise debug mode used early on.

Haystack 2.0 was rebuilt with production debugging in mind, adding structured logging with built-in tracing correlation plus a Hayhooks deployment layer that auto-generates REST schemas from pipeline introspection.
LlamaIndex's instrumentation module tracks spans and events through a dispatcher/handler system, giving visibility into retrieval and generation steps.

Framework-agnostic tools like OpenLLMetry and Traceloop can observe vector-database and LLM calls regardless of orchestration layer, which matters if debugging tooling needs to survive a later framework swap.

For evaluation, RAGAS (faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision/recall) and TruLens's RAG Triad (context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance) are the two most established metric sets, and both work largely without hand-labeled ground truth.
The broader tooling landscape also includes Phoenix, DeepEval, LangSmith, and OpenAI Evals, implementing similar metrics with different integration depth into specific frameworks.
LlamaIndex bakes several of these same categories directly into its own evaluation modules, so adopting it for retrieval yields evaluation largely for free.

DSPy is a fundamentally different tool and should be treated as an optimization layer rather than an orchestration replacement: it separates program flow from prompt/weight parameters and uses optimizers plus Assertions to tune prompts against a metric you define.

This is documented to work best in English and to struggle with very complex, highly detailed task instructions, making DSPy a reasonable second-stage investment once evaluation data exists rather than a first production framework.

On avoiding a framework mess later, a practical account of running Haystack, LangChain, and LlamaIndex in production concluded that a custom, dependency-light integration is often the better call, ranking Haystack as the most stable off-the-shelf option and LangChain as flexible but prone to breaking changes across updates.

A more architectural warning is that the biggest lock-in risk is not the vendor chosen but building a universal LLM abstraction at the model-API layer, which forces a lowest-common-denominator interface and blocks fast adoption of new provider features; the fix is keeping any abstraction aligned to specific product user stories instead of to models.

This argues for using LangChain's components selectively, since its own strength is that pieces can be used independently of the full framework, while keeping the assistant's core logic in your own code so a future migration touches call sites rather than the whole application.

Even LangGraph's own comparison discussion acknowledges the broader criticism that LLM frameworks tend to "over-complicate things," reinforcing that added abstraction should be adopted deliberately per capability, not wholesale.

Putting this together for a first production version: build the RAG and agent core in Python using LangChain plus LangGraph for tool-calling over ticket/doc data and admin APIs, instrumented with LangSmith for tracing and RAGAS/TruLens for evaluation.
If retrieval quality over product docs is the primary bottleneck, swap in LlamaIndex's indexing/retrieval layer under that same orchestration rather than replacing the whole stack.

Expose the.NET billing/admin systems as narrow REST endpoints that the Python agent calls as tools, and only reach for Semantic Kernel on the.NET side later if native in-process C# AI orchestration is needed.

Hold off on DSPy and on a dependency-free rebuild until real evaluation data exists and a concrete pain point remains, then let those metrics decide between DSPy-style optimization or a leaner custom layer.
